### A fixed primitive receiver supports reliable coded communication

For asymptotically reliable communication, the receiver need not become more accurate on every use as the coding block grows.

Choose one finite receiver program with error below a sufficient coding threshold. Keep that primitive fixed. With fresh source inputs, pure incident fields and receiver resets, it supplies an iid noisy quantum link.

The explicit attained protocol is:

1. Send halves of locally prepared Bell pairs through the primitive.
2. Apply independent bilateral Pauli twirls.
3. Use the preserved acquired quantum-expander-code family and small-set-flip decoding.
4. Distill Bell pairs and teleport the later unknown payload.

The Fawzi–Grospellier–Leverrier theorem supplies a positive random-error threshold and efficient decoding for the underlying constant-rate code family. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

The retained acquisition uses random lifts of \(K_{384,192}\). At the allowed block lengths,

\[
n=5(192q)^2,\qquad k\ge n/5.
\]

The construction charges graph-acquisition failure, random-sampling abort and decoding failure explicitly. It yields an asymptotic rate of at least **\(1/5\) payload qubit per primitive use**, once the fixed primitive is sufficiently accurate.

This is a **classical-assisted** attained protocol. Twirling keys, syndrome exchange and teleportation messages are counted. The code buffers grow as \(O(n)\); a sufficient generic local Clifford gate bound is \(O(n^2)\). Sequential collection entails \(O(nT)\) coherent waiting before other local processing and latency. Consequently, the rate per primitive use does not by itself establish a laboratory rate per second.

A trusted local Bell-parity test also provides an operational calibration procedure. It tests the actual emitted pairs, with finite confidence, instead of inferring receiver access from a reduced generator. It assumes iid operation and trusted local measurements; finite data do not establish those assumptions automatically.
